journal_name: International Journal of Education and the Arts
title: Artificial Intelligence and Human Arts Educators as Collaborators
abstract: The arts are anchored in human creativity, expression and interpretation. The introduction of generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) challenges traditional notions of creativity, authorship, and emotional intelligence, prompting arts educators to consider its place in the classroom. In this pilot, six tertiary arts educators and three generative AI platforms (ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot), answered the question: how can AI improve arts education? Using Deleuze and Guattari’s rhizomatic analysis, we mapped convergences, divergences, and silences across human and non-human actors. The paper contributes to understanding how integrated human creativity and technological advancements can support students, reveals potential directions for practice and research, and raises concerns that must be mitigated regarding equity of access and AI literacy.

journal_name: International Journal of Education and the Arts
title: Lived Experience of Time in High School Musical Theater
abstract: This phenomenological study investigated the lived experience of rehearsing for and performing in a high school musical. Following van Manen's hermeneutic phenomenological method and using data from interviews and reflective journals with five student performers, the research explored how some students experience high school musical theater as a bounded, set-apart period of time separate from regular academic activities, a theme that emerged through phenomenological inquiry. Findings included that learning in musical theater extended beyond traditional skill acquisition, encompassing a transformative process of becoming a musical theater participant. Students’ most meaningful learning occurred in liminal spaces, suggesting musical theater offers a profound, identity-shaping encounter.

journal_name: International Journal of Education and the Arts
title: Integrating Art and Science in Education
abstract: STEAM education has gained increasing attention as an interdisciplinary approach that integrates the arts to enrich science learning and foster creative thinking. This study examines how combining artistic creation with scientific experimentation promotes students’ creative expression, inquisitive thinking, and emotional engagement. The study utilized an art-based action research methodology, conducted over two months, with 20 first-grade students in China. Data were collected through the researcher’s observation diary, students’ artworks, oral reflections, and photographic documentation of the instructional process. Data analysis involved reflective observation and interpretation to examine how students engaged with scientific concepts through creativity. The findings suggest that integrating art and science through multisensory activities promotes creative expression, fosters inquisitive thinking, and enhances emotional engagement, engaging with scientific phenomena in exploratory ways.

journal_name: International Journal of Education and the Arts
title: Voicing Identity Through Puppetry
abstract: This qualitative study explores the pedagogical and expressive potential of puppetry as an embodied, arts-based practice in adult English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learning. Situated within sociocultural, embodied, and arts-based perspectives, the study examines how puppet-mediated interaction shapes oral expression, creativity, and identity negotiation among adult learners. Adopting a performative qualitative case study design, the research was conducted over a six-week puppetry-based program in a private language institute. Data generated through puppet performances, semi-structured interviews, reflective journals, and classroom observations suggest that puppetry can reduce affective barriers such as anxiety and self-consciousness, enabling learners to engage in risk-taking and sustained discourse. Participants’ narratives indicate that puppetry functioned as a “third space” for identity experimentation, allowing learners to project alternative voices and negotiate social positioning in the target language. The multimodal and playful nature of puppetry supported learner agency by engaging affective, social, and embodied dimensions of language use. Overall, the study contributes

journal_name: International Journal of Education and the Arts
title: Please: Choose This Adventure
abstract: Laura Kapalka Richerme’s Popular Music Will Not Save Us presents readers with an examination of the intersections of capitalism and music education that is both depressing and enlightening. Despite the provocative title, the question this worthy contribution asks is not whether popular music can save music education, but whether anything can save music education from capitalism. Readers benefit from Richerme’s thorough review of the origins and current state of capitalism, as well as the affective flows that are suggested as an alternative to genre as a tool that may deflect the impact of capitalism in the classroom and more equitably center the students. In the style of a “Choose Your Own Adventure” book, Richerme presents four positions that music educators can take in order to maneuver a landscape dominated by capitalism: to thrive, survive, resist, or challenge.

journal_name: International Journal of Education and the Arts
title: From Oral Histories to Archival Songs
abstract: Music education scholars have increasingly advocated for critical and creative pedagogies that amplify marginalized voices and integrate lived experiences through various forms of knowledge and production. Songwriting offers a compelling opportunity to bridge artistic expression and academic inquiry. This article examines the methodological and pedagogical implications of songwriting archival songs as a creative-critical tool for music and social studies educators and researchers, highlighting its potential to activate emotional and cognitive engagement while (re)constructing historical memory through sonic imagination. Oral history interviews with Italian Resistance women were transformed into archival songs, sound collage artifacts that connected and interpreted emotions, stories, and themes, activating rememory as a mode of collective historical uncovering. Performed at a public library, these songs served as creative artifacts fostering affective engagement and critical reflection. Findings suggest that archival songs position creativity as the generative force that precedes criticality at the heart of a critical-creative pedagogy.

journal_name: International Journal of Education and the Arts
title: Managing Art-based Extracurriculars
abstract: This study investigates the role of educational management in supporting drama and performance-based extracurricular activities in Nigerian secondary schools, with a focus on student perceptions. In an educational context where formal curricula often prioritize cognitive outcomes over creative expression, arts-based extracurriculars offer critical platforms for holistic development. Despite their transformative potential in fostering socio-emotional learning, identity exploration, and civic engagement, such programs are frequently marginalized due to weak institutional support and ineffective administrative practices. Grounded in Aesthetic Leadership Theory and Lived Curriculum Theory, this research explores how school leadership either enables or constrains student access to these creative outlets. Employing a quantitative methodology, the study surveyed junior secondary students from selected schools in Enugu State. Findings aim to illuminate the level of student participation, their perceptions of administrative support, and the personal benefits gained from drama involvement. journal_name: International Journal of Education and the Arts
title: Addressing Anti-Black Racism in Ballet
abstract: Ballet is a beloved art form around the world, but issues of anti-Black racism are pervasive within ballet’s culture and repertoire. In 2023, Canada’s National Ballet School (NBS) initiated Assemblée Internationale 2023 (AI23), a series of events guided by the NOFS framework (Name, Own, Frame, Sustain) to support leading ballet schools in addressing anti-Black racism in their organizations. The purpose of this study was to investigate the impact of AI23 on participants’ understanding of systemic anti-Black racism in ballet’s practices. The study employed mixed-methods, including online surveys and focus groups. Results demonstrated AI23 helped participants Name issues of anti-Black racism in ballet and consider ways to Frame changes that need to be made in the sector. However, Owning individual/institutional responsibility for systemic anti-Black racism and Sustaining change over time was not realized. Future work to continue efforts initiated by AI23 and utility of the NOFS framework are considered.

journal_name: International Journal of Education and the Arts
title: Explicit Teaching Mandates
abstract: This article critiques the universal application of explicit instruction mandates in Australian education, arguing they misalign with the embodied and experiential nature of arts learning. These mandates, based on a narrow evidence-base dominated by cognitive load theory (CLT), promote pedagogies that isolate the brain from the body, neglecting the integral role of the body in learning. While explicit instruction is effective in certain contexts, its universal application disregards the complexities of teaching and learning, especially in practice-based subjects such as the arts. Such approaches risk disengaging students, undermining creativity, and ignoring the aesthetic and embodied practices central to arts education. The article calls for a broader evidence base that includes embodied cognition and advocates for discipline-specific approaches that honor the embodied, aesthetic, and experiential nature of arts learning. It urges arts educators to use their expertise to influence policy and ensure meaningful, engaged learning.

journal_name: International Journal of Education and the Arts
title: Echoes in Translation
abstract: This article explores the potential of poetic inquiry to re-read Vietnamese English as a foreign language (EFL) teachers’ reflective writing as affective, ethical, and aesthetic texts. Drawing from two datasets, including private reflections collected during professional development and public-facing teaching innovation entries, the study rearranges teacher-authored lines into found poems, organized into five thematic cycles: (1) becoming, (2) constraints and care, (3) voice and silence, (4) recognition and innovation, and (5) teaching across languages. Rather than thematically coding or categorizing the data, this inquiry foregrounds rhythm, pause, metaphor, and relational weight. It treats reflective writing not only as a source of pedagogical insight but as a genre of professional authorship. The article includes a dialogic commentary and comparative discussion that situate this poetic mode within broader traditions of narrative inquiry, teacher identity research, and arts-based methods. In doing so, we argue for listening differently to what teachers say, and to how their words live beyond the analytic frame.

journal_name: International Journal of Education and the Arts
title: Belonging in Motion
abstract: This study revisits student perceptions of diversity, inclusion, and equity in postsecondary dance programs, building on our earlier research from 2015. While curricular changes—such as the inclusion of hip hop and other global diaspora forms—suggest progress, students continue to identify gaps in representation, particularly in performances and public events. These outward-facing spaces often send stronger messages about program values than course catalogs, influencing students’ sense of belonging. As dance education evolves alongside shifting socio-political climates and institutional pressures, this current research examines how students experience inclusion both in the classroom and on stage. We argue that dance programs must critically assess how selection processes, performance venues, and programming reflect inclusive values and support culturally meaningful representation. By centering student voices, this study highlights both the momentum toward equity and the persistent challenges in creating truly inclusive dance education environments.

journal_name: International Journal of Education and the Arts
title: Writing and Art as Emotional Connection Tools in a Postcard Workshop
abstract: This study explores the impact of handwriting on the emotional experience of university students within an arts-based educational context that integrates drawing and visual intervention as catalysts for reflective and affective writing. Using a critical phenomenological approach, 116 students participated in a writing and drawing workshop inspired by Saul Steinberg’s postcards, created in a context of displacement. Data were collected through a 17-question open-ended survey and analyzed with Atlas.ti. Results indicate that handwriting enhances emotional expression, message clarity, and emotional bonds, surpassing digital communication, especially in physical formats. An implication of the study is to recover the value of handwriting in education and integrate it as a tool to foster reflection and emotional connection. The limitations of the study address the small sample size and the qualitative approach, which restricts the generalization of the results.

journal_name: International Journal of Education and the Arts
title: Ballroom Choreography as a Means of Shaping Cultural and Aesthetic Values in University Students
abstract: This study aimed to explore the developmental influence of a ballroom choreography programme – operating through the fundamental precepts of Dance/Movement Therapy – on aesthetic-emotional sensitivity, somatic awareness, orientation towards culturally prescribed values, and interpersonal empathy among university undergraduates. Participants (N = 124) were undergraduate choreography students divided into an experimental group (n = 58) that participated in a 16-session choreographic intervention and a control group (n = 66) that received no such training. Standardised tools were employed pre- and post-intervention: Emotional-Aesthetic Sensitivity Scale (EAS), Rokeach Value Survey (RVS), Body Awareness Questionnaire (BAQ), and Interpersonal Reactivity Index (IRI). Paired and independent-sample t-tests and MANOVA were used for data analysis. Results are presented about recent theories on embodied learning, aesthetic mutuality, and choreographic pedagogy.

journal_name: International Journal of Education and the Arts
title: A/R/Tography in Reception Settings:
abstract: This arts-based research, grounded in an a/r/tographic approach, explores how collaborative artistic practices in a Spanish reception center foster personal expression, social integration, and meaning-making among 53 African male migrants. Through workshops that combined symbolic self-portraits, cultural maps, performances, and photovoice, participants developed creative, expressive, and social competencies while generating visual and narrative artifacts that conveyed complex migratory experiences beyond verbal interviews. The project integrated participant observation, visual and narrative analysis, and community return via the itinerant exhibition Voces de la migración [Voices of Migration], positioning art both as research data and public pedagogy. Findings highlight the potential of non-formal, culturally situated art education to promote resilience, intercultural dialogue, and social cohesion, aligning with UNESCO's Road Map for Arts Education and the UN Sustainable Development Goals. journal_name: International Journal of Education and the Arts
title: Bejoli, A Cultural Performance: Manifestations of Resistance, Identity, and Community Education in a Village in South Sumatra, Indonesia
abstract: In response to the declining engagement of younger generations in traditional rituals and the cultural commodification of local performances, this article explores the Bejoli tradition in Kuang Dalam Village, South Sumatra, Indonesia, as a form of community-based performance art that acts as cultural resistance, reinforces local identity, and serves as a site for intergenerational nonformal pedagogy. Using performative ethnography, this study investigates how Bejoli functions as an experiential learning space, enabling embodied learning beyond formal institutions. The analysis shows that Bejoli endures not only as an aesthetic ritual but as a dynamic platform where generations interact to transmit social values, local spirituality, and cultural awareness. Despite globalization and modern shifts, the core meaning of Bejoli remains intact due to selective cultural reflection. This study highlights the significance of community arts as dynamic, participatory, and relevant educational platforms for maintaining identity amid cultural homogenization.

journal_name: International Journal of Education and the Arts
title: Living Art as Essential: A Case Study of a Living Composer’s Music in a High School Orchestra
abstract: This study explores the issues surrounding living composers’ music, its pedagogical application in teaching, and the potential benefits and challenges it presents. Drawing on Westerlund and López-Íñiguez’s (2025) concept of practice in context, which emphasizes the interconnectedness of artistic work and its broader social, institutional, and educational environments, this research positions contemporary music not only as a musical product but as a socially embedded practice. Through an extensive qualitative case study conducted over a six-month period, the implementation of a contemporary music piece, composed by the orchestra director, within a high school arts program was examined. The findings revealed both challenges and rewards. The director’s tailored pedagogy to individual students emerged as a necessary step in promoting living art. Students initially faced difficulty engaging with the unfamiliar tonal language, complex rhythms, and notational demands of the piece, compounded by limited prior exposure to living composers’ music. journal_name: International Journal of Education and the Arts
title: “Sometimes You Don’t Even Know What’s Inside Your Own Neighborhood”: Critical and Creative Cartographies in Art Education
abstract: The understanding of maps as representations of the subjective, interpersonal, social and political realities of individuals and collectives is a valuable insight for art education. In this article, I explore cartographic practices that enable collective and individual expression of narratives and identities in relation to place. I explore the theoretical underpinnings of such approaches, provide artistic and educational examples, and describe my research on the integration of creative cartographies in high school art classrooms. In interviews with students and analysis of their collective maps, there was evidence that students learned about their everyday environments by designing and going on walks, and photographically documenting their neighborhoods. Students also learned from and about each other by sharing geo-tagged images on collective online maps. These examples provide some insights for educators and researchers on the value of integrating critical and creative cartographies for gaining spatial understandings and enabling spatial conversations.

journal_name: International Journal of Education and the Arts
title: Arts Education, Wellbeing and Leisure: Australian Primary Teacher Education Student Views
abstract: Arts Education fosters personal development and cultivates opportunities for students to be creative and innovative. This research forms part of a wider study, Emerging issues and directions in Arts Education: Perceptions and capacities of Initial Teacher Education students. The authors draw on survey data (September–October 2024) (n = 60) in Australia to explore teacher education students’ perceptions of the ways in which Arts Education contributes to wellbeing. Data were coded using thematic analysis where two themes are discussed. The findings show a strong connection between on-campus study and online Arts learning. It confirmed that active participation in leisurely activities is personally fulfilling and rewarding, contributing to student wellbeing. As the small sample size is a limitation, generalisations cannot be made. This study adds to the wider body of research regarding the impact of Arts Education on wellbeing.

journal_name: International Journal of Education and the Arts
title: Sketching As an Embodied Cognitive Process in Craft Education
abstract: This study explores how pre-service and in-service craft teachers perceive and utilize sketching as a cognitive, pedagogical, and embodied tool in craft education. Drawing on the theoretical framework of Embodied Cognition, the research positions sketching as a material and multimodal practice that bridges abstract thinking and hands-on making. Data was collected through a survey distributed to craft educators, and analyzed thematically using concepts such as cognitive offloading, material engagement, and affordances. The findings reveal that teachers view sketching as an important support for student planning, problem-solving, and reflection. However, the degree to which sketching is actively integrated into teaching varies widely. While some educators scaffold sketching through modelling and dialogue, others rely on implicit or ad-hoc approaches. The study also highlights challenges in motivating students who resist sketching or perceive it as irrelevant. These insights underscore the need for pedagogical strategies that position sketching as an inclusive, flexible, and epistemically rich practice.
